slides: Open by naming the chapter's tension: a symplectic form is locally as rigid as the standard matrix, but the moment it is used to move functions and submanifolds it becomes a dynamics engine. Tell students that the lecture follows the notebook's computational route, not a list of isolated definitions.

Use the route map as a dependency diagram. The left column supplies algebra and exterior calculus, the middle column builds canonical and local models, and the right column records what becomes testable: Lagrangian graphs, conserved quantities, and first-order PDEs.

Pause on the matrix before giving the manifold definition. The key distinction from a metric is that the tensor is skew and area-pairing, yet nondegenerate. The notebook check says determinant one, J squared is minus the identity, and the top wedge coefficient is two in dimension four.

Emphasize that the complement S^omega is not Euclidean orthogonality. The table is useful because it shows every classification coming from exact rank, dimension, and containment tests. Lagrangian means both isotropic and coisotropic here, not merely half-dimensional by accident.

Frame cotangent bundles as the universal example. The tautological one-form remembers the covector being evaluated, and its exterior derivative gives the canonical symplectic form. The graph computation is the cleanest local test: closed one-forms give Lagrangian graphs, nonclosed ones leave a residual.

Present Darboux as a proof mechanism rather than a magic coordinate theorem. Moser's path converts the problem into finding a time-dependent vector field whose contraction cancels the changing two-form. The radial field in the artifact is a concrete local witness for that cancellation.

For Hamiltonian dynamics, make the sign convention explicit and then point to the oscillator. The vector field stays tangent to energy level curves because dH along X_H is zero. Poisson brackets package the same idea for two functions, with angular momentum commuting with the isotropic oscillator Hamiltonian.

This slide is the bridge out of pure symplectic geometry. A Hamilton-Jacobi equation is solved by building a Lagrangian flowout, then reading it as a closed one-form and lifting to a jet. The contact form test says the one-jet is Legendrian exactly when it really came from a function.

Treat the lab as four stress tests, and slow the class down before anyone computes. For each row, first ask: which theorem or construction was quietly using this hypothesis? Then let the residue name the failure. A nonclosed one-form graph does not merely look less canonical; its pullback of the symplectic form leaves a coefficient behind, so the Lagrangian test fails in the most literal way. A degenerate Moser model shows why Darboux needs a genuinely invertible two-form throughout the local argument. The anisotropic oscillator is a dynamics warning: once rotational symmetry is broken, angular momentum has a nonzero Poisson bracket with the Hamiltonian and stops being conserved. Finally, the Hamilton-Jacobi denominator marks where the local generating function ceases to be single-valued. The teaching goal is diagnostic fluency: students should connect each failed hypothesis to the exact artifact residual they can inspect after class.

Close by asking students to name the hypothesis behind each tool. Nondegeneracy gives complements and Hamiltonian vector fields; closedness gives Darboux and Lagrangian graph tests; Poisson brackets detect conservation; contact geometry records the PDE endpoint.
